_comment: Platform-level reference data used across the site. Compatibility labels describe the platform as a whole and are not a per-ROM test result.

arcade.name: MAME / Arcade
arcade.tagline: Coin-op classics, one cabinet at a time
arcade.description: Stand-up arcade boards running everything from vector shooters to four-player brawlers, preserved as MAME ROM sets.
arcade.longDescription: The arcade group is the largest part of the collection and holds two kinds of entry: unpacked ROM-set folders (such as DKONG) and zipped ROM sets (such as sf2.zip). Both are MAME-style sets, and MAME expects the archive or folder name to match the driver name exactly. Arcade hardware changed constantly between 1978 and the mid-1990s, so each set emulates a different board — from a 1 MHz 8080 to 16-bit dual-68000 systems.
arcade.hardware: Original arcade printed circuit boards, emulated in MAME
arcade.emulator: MAME (standalone) or FinalBurn Neo / MAME cores inside RetroArch
arcade.compatibilityNote: Arcade sets must match the emulator's ROM set version. A set that runs in one MAME release can fail in another; the ROM set is only as good as the driver that expects it.
arcade.piModels: Pi 4 (2 GB+) or Pi 5 recommended. Pi 3B+ handles most pre-1986 titles; Pi Zero 2 W is best limited to early 8-bit boards.
arcade.controller: Keyboard, arcade stick or any USB/Bluetooth gamepad. Twin-stick titles (Robotron, Black Widow) need two analogue sticks or a dual-stick layout.
arcade.install: Install MAME through RetroPie's package manager or RetroArch's online updater, then place each ROM set in the arcade ROM directory without renaming it.

nes.name: Nintendo Entertainment System
nes.description: Nintendo's 8-bit home console, home to platformers, RPGs and a huge library of licensed and unlicensed cartridges.
nes.longDescription: The NES group is made up of .nes ROM images named after their cartridges. The filenames mix styles — some use No-Intro conventions, others use underscores or short abbreviations — so RB Hub normalises them for display while keeping the original filename intact. The library includes emulator files such as BioNES.exe and Nesticle.pal in the same folder; those are excluded from the Game Library.
nes.hardware: Ricoh 2A03 (6502-derived) CPU with the NES PPU
nes.emulator: Nestopia or FCEUmm (RetroArch); Mesen2 for accuracy
nes.compatibilityNote: NES emulation is lightweight and well documented at full speed on a Pi 3 or newer. Mapper support is the main variable: unusual or homebrew mappers may need a specific core.
nes.piModels: Pi 3B+, Pi 4 or Pi 5. Even a Pi Zero 2 W can run most NES titles.
nes.controller: Any gamepad. A NES-style pad suits the two-button layout; Zapper games need a mouse or a compatible light gun.
nes.install: Install lr-nestopia or lr-fceumm through RetroPie, or load the Nestopia core in RetroArch, then copy .nes files into the nes ROM folder.

snes.name: Super Nintendo Entertainment System
snes.description: Nintendo's 16-bit console, with the collection's compressed No-Intro sets plus loose .sfc and .smc files.
snes.longDescription: The SNES group mixes zipped No-Intro sets (alphabetically A–D in the source inventory) with loose .sfc and .smc ROM images for a set of well-known titles. Filename tags such as (USA), (Japan), (Europe), (Rev 1), (Proto) and (Beta) identify the dump and are listed as variants on each game page.
snes.hardware: Ricoh 5A22 (65816-derived) with the SPC700 sound chip
snes.emulator: Snes9x (retroarch core) or bsnes for higher accuracy
snes.compatibilityNote: Standard cartridges run well on a Pi 4. Games using enhancement chips (Super FX, SA-1, DSP-1) and some fan hacks need a specific core and may dip below full speed.
snes.piModels: Pi 4 or Pi 5 recommended; Pi 3B+ is adequate for most titles without enhancement chips.
snes.controller: A SNES-style pad with four face buttons and two shoulder buttons covers every control scheme in the library.
snes.install: Install lr-snes9x via RetroPie or load Snes9x in RetroArch, then place the .zip/.sfc/.smc files in the snes ROM folder — compressed sets can be used directly.

atari2600.name: Atari 2600
atari2600.tagline: The console that started the cartridge era
atari2600.description: Atari's 1977 console, represented by twelve .bin cartridge images of arcade ports and original Activision classics.
atari2600.longDescription: The Atari 2600 group holds twelve .bin cartridge dumps. The files use both .bin and .BIN extensions, which are equivalent; the emulator does not care about case. Every title here is a genuine cartridge release, including the Parker Brothers Frogger port and Activision's Pitfall!.
atari2600.hardware: MOS 6507 CPU with the TIA video/audio chip
atari2600.compatibilityNote: The 2600 is one of the lightest systems to emulate; Stella has run at full speed on Raspberry Pi hardware since the Pi 2.
atari2600.piModels: Any model from Pi 3 onward. Pi Zero and Pi Zero 2 W also cope comfortably.
atari2600.controller: A single-button joystick is enough. Paddle games such as Kaboom! need an analogue paddle or a mouse mapped to paddle input.
atari2600.install: Install Stella (lr-stella) through RetroPie or RetroArch, then copy .bin files into the atari2600 ROM folder.

gba.name: Game Boy Advance
gba.description: Nintendo's 32-bit handheld, represented here by seven .gba titles including Pokémon, Fire Emblem and Mother 3.
gba.longDescription: The Game Boy Advance group contains seven .gba ROM images. Several are Japan-only releases (Fire Emblem: Fūin no Tsurugi and Mother 3), which matters when looking for legitimate copies. The library stores the filename exactly as it appears in the inventory.
gba.hardware: ARM7TDMI with a custom 2D graphics chip
gba.emulator: mGBA (retroarch core) or gpSP on lighter setups
gba.compatibilityNote: mGBA runs most GBA software at full speed on a Pi 4. Real-time-clock features in the Pokémon games depend on the core's RTC setting.
gba.piModels: Pi 4 or Pi 5 recommended; Pi 3B+ handles most titles with mGBA.
gba.controller: A pad with A, B, L, R and Start/Select. Pokémon and Fire Emblem also use the shoulder buttons heavily.
gba.install: Install lr-mgba through RetroPie or RetroArch, then copy .gba files into the gba ROM folder.

nds.name: Nintendo DS
nds.description: Nintendo's dual-screen handheld. The inventory contains a single .nds game, Mario Kart DS, plus a save file.
nds.longDescription: The Nintendo DS group contains one game image (Mario Kart DS) and one .dsv save file. The save file is a DeSmuME memory card and is not a game, so it is excluded from the library. Dual-screen emulation needs more processing power than the other handhelds in this collection.
nds.hardware: ARM9 + ARM7 dual-processor design with two LCD screens
nds.compatibilityNote: DS emulation is the heaviest handheld target here. Expect to tune resolution scaling and frameskip on a Pi 4, and expect some titles to remain unplayable.
nds.piModels: Pi 4 (4 GB+) or Pi 5. Pi 3-class hardware is not a realistic target for DS emulation.
nds.controller: A gamepad plus touch input. Many DS games expect a stylus, which is mapped to the mouse or the right analogue stick on most builds.
nds.install: Install lr-melonds through RetroPie's experimental packages, or run melonDS standalone, then copy .nds files into the nds ROM folder.

n64.name: Nintendo 64
n64.description: Nintendo's 64-bit console, with four games in the inventory including Super Mario 64 and Majora's Mask.
n64.longDescription: The N64 group contains four games plus save files (.eep and .mpk) that are excluded from the library. Super Smash Bros. is stored as a folder in the source listing, so its contents are not itemised. N64 emulation is the most demanding target in this collection.
n64.hardware: NEC VR4300 MIPS processor with the Reality Coprocessor
n64.compatibilityNote: Frame rate and compatibility vary enormously between plugins and per-game settings. A Pi 4 can run several titles acceptably with tuning; a Pi 5 is a better starting point.
n64.piModels: Pi 5 recommended. Pi 4 (4 GB+) can run some titles with reduced resolution and frameskip.
n64.controller: An N64-style pad with analogue stick and four C-buttons is ideal; a modern twin-stick pad works with a remap.
n64.install: Install lr-mupen64plus-next through RetroPie, then copy .n64/.z64 files into the n64 ROM folder and adjust the per-game core options.

homebrew.name: Homebrew (LÖVE)
homebrew.tagline: Indie games outside the console world
homebrew.description: A single homebrew .love package, Mari0 — a fan-made mash-up of Super Mario Bros. and Portal.
homebrew.longDescription: The love folder contains one file, mari0.love. A .love file is a zip archive containing Lua source and assets for the LÖVE framework, not a console ROM. It runs natively on Linux, so on a Raspberry Pi it needs the LÖVE runtime rather than an emulator.
homebrew.emulator: No emulator — the LÖVE runtime executes it natively
homebrew.compatibilityNote: Native Linux software rather than emulation. Performance depends on the Pi model and on whether the game's OpenGL requirements are met by the desktop environment.
homebrew.piModels: Pi 4 or Pi 5 with a desktop environment and working OpenGL drivers.
homebrew.controller: Keyboard and mouse as designed; gamepads can be mapped through the LÖVE joystick API.
homebrew.install: Install the love package from your distribution's repository, then run 'love mari0.love' from a terminal.
